title: Cross-referencing Tasmanian Terrestrial Ecosystems
text:
Overview of this document
This document presents a reproducible computational workflow for the analysis and synthesis of cross-referencing information for Tasmanian terrestrial and transitional ecosystems. Cross-referencing aims to elucidate explicit, evidence-based relationships between units of ecosystem classifications that represent comparable entities , see 1  Stepwise cross-referencing process.
The repository serves a dual purpose:
In this workflow, the source classification is the TASVEG 5.0 dataset (Tasmanian Vegetation Monitoring and Mapping Program 2025; Kitchener and Harris 2013), whose technical manual and fire-attributes lookup table define 159 mapping units (156 mapped as polygons across mainland Tasmania and surrounding islands), most of which represent ecological vegetation communities (see 2  Source classification: TASVEG). These vegetation communities are aligned with the ecosystem concept of the target classification, the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (IUCN GET; Keith et al. (2022); see 3  Assess alignment between classifications), specifically at Level 3 (Ecosystem Functional Groups, EFGs).
The main body of the document is organised into three parts:
Appendices provide a glossary of cross-referencing terminology, a reference on tabular membership formats (15  Membership data formats), R session and benchmarking notes (16  Reproducibility of R code), and an overview table summarising the status of all published, draft, and in-development workflow outputs (17  Overview of workflow outputs).
This online document is a joint output of the ARDC “Ecosystem Indicators Workflows” (EIW) project and the ARC Industry Laureate Fellowship Project “Foundations for leading the nature positive ecosystem conservation agenda”.
You can use the links on the left to navigate through the different sections of this resource.

title: Cross-referencing Tasmanian Terrestrial Ecosystems
text:
Reproducibility statement
This resource uses Bash and R for data download, preparation, analysis, and synthesis, and is rendered as a Quarto book following FAIR data and research software principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016; Barker et al. 2022). All analytical steps in the documentation are reproducible from the tracked expert elicitation tables (xrefdata/) and publicly available TASVEG 5.0 spatial data (gisdata/). Standalone spatial output scripts are separated in scripts/ so computationally expensive rasterisation and vector-union steps are not repeated unnecessarily when updating the documentation. Instructions for environment setup, benchmarking logs, and FAIR assessment notes are provided in 16  Reproducibility of R code and 17  Overview of workflow outputs.

title: 1  Stepwise cross-referencing process
text:
1.1 Overview of the stepwise cross-referencing process
The need to cross-reference different ecosystem classification systems arises frequently in ecological research, national ecosystem accounting, Red List of Ecosystems assessments, and conservation reporting. The conceptual foundations, standards, and diagnostic methods for cross-referencing classifications to the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (IUCN GET; Keith et al. (2022)) are established in IUCN (2025).
Here we apply consistent standards and reproducible computational methods so that relationships between classification units are explicit, auditable, and straightforward to update whenever new ecological evidence or updated spatial maps become available. Formalising the cross-referencing pipeline also minimises undocumented or divergent interpretations when local vegetation typologies are translated into global reporting frameworks (De Cáceres and Wiser 2012; IUCN 2025).
Cross-referencing links a source classification to a target classification, where the target classification typically has a broader thematic or geographic scope than the source. Each unit in the source classification can relate directly to one or more units in the target classification. Following fuzzy set theory (Zadeh 1965) and the IUCN guidelines (IUCN 2025), this relationship is quantified using fuzzy membership values between 0 (0%, excluded) and 1 (100%, unambiguous assignment), summing to 1 across all assigned target units for a given source unit and interpreter.
Combining independent membership assessments from multiple domain experts—structured across iterative elicitation rounds with facilitated discussion between rounds—reduces linguistic ambiguity, guards against individual cognitive biases, and yields robust, transparent estimates of both consensus and residual thematic uncertainty (Martin et al. 2012; Hemming et al. 2018).
A five-step diagnostic process ensures that the cross-referencing exercise upholds four core principles: (1) conceptual alignment of classifications, (2) membership estimation based on entity properties, (3) weight of evidence, and (4) transparent representation of uncertainty (IUCN 2025).

title: 1  Stepwise cross-referencing process
text:
Figure 1.1: Structure of the stepwise cross-referencing process adapted from IUCN (2025).




Steps 1 and 2 establish conceptual eligibility and assemble the ecological and spatial reference information that underpins all subsequent decisions.
Steps 3 and 4 involve multiple domain experts independently eliminating implausible target units and estimating non-zero fuzzy memberships. Conducting a second round of elicitation after structured group discussion (analogous to the Investigate–Discuss–Estimate–Aggregate, or IDEA, protocol; Hemming et al. (2018)) typically involves:

gathering independent first-round expert contributions,
analysing inter-interpreter discrepancies, target usage, and uncertainty to guide structured discussion, and
collecting revised second-round contributions from each interpreter.

Step 5 synthesises the validated multi-interpreter membership tables into summary tables, spatial area estimates, and geospatial outputs, while documenting remaining sources of uncertainty.

title: 1  Stepwise cross-referencing process
text:
1.2 Reproducible computational workflow
This repository assists in the translation of parts of the conceptual process in Figure 1.1 into a reproducible computational workflow.


While the computation workflow is reproducible for correctly formatted input data, we stress that these steps cannot be decoupled from the expert elicitation process. Ultimately all inputs and outputs have to be checked and reviewed by the human expert with the ecosystem specific knowledge to make correct decisions and interpretations.
The workflow takes raw interpreter spreadsheets (xrefdata/) and authoritative TASVEG 5.0 spatial data (gisdata/), executes validation and analysis steps transparently in R, and produces versioned, FAIR-aligned data products (Wilkinson et al. 2016; Barker et al. 2022).
We build on the ecoSynthesis R package (Ferrer-Paris, Gould, and Singh 2026)—currently under active development—together with repository-specific helper functions in scripts/functions.R and standard spatial/tidyverse packages. Throughout this book, explicit call-out notes highlight where package functions and repository helpers overlap or differ, explaining which implementation is preferred at each step.
To keep documentation rendering fast and modular, the analytical Quarto workflow (docs-src/) is kept separate from the standalone output-generation scripts (scripts/), which perform computationally heavier tasks such as 90 m rasterisation (fasterize) and statewide GeoPackage assembly (see Chapter 17).
Within the analytical workflow, we distinguish two main computational stages: (1) Data preparation, validation, and exploration, and (2) Analysis and synthesis (see Figure 1.2).

text:
1.3 Structure of this document

Preliminaries: Source classification overview (Chapter 2) and conceptual alignment to IUCN GET (Chapter 3).
Part I — Preparation: Lookup tables (Chapter 4), reading heterogeneous membership tables (Chapter 5), validation and cleaning (Chapter 6), and initial data exploration (Chapter 7).
Part II — Analysis: Within-round agreement, target usage, and Shannon’s entropy for Round 1 (Chapter 8) and Round 2 (Chapter 9), followed by between-round comparisons (Chapter 10).
Part III — Synthesis: Membership synthesis strategies (Chapter 11), unweighted and weighted area summaries (Chapter 12), and spatial output concepts (Chapter 13).
Appendices: Glossary, membership table formats (Chapter 15), R reproducibility and benchmarking notes (Chapter 16), and the status overview of all repository outputs (Chapter 17).

title: 2  Source classification: TASVEG
text:
2.1 Components of TASVEG used in this workflow
In this workflow, the source classification is TASVEG, the comprehensive digital vegetation map and classification system for Tasmania, including sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island (Tasmanian Vegetation Monitoring and Mapping Program 2013, 2025).
The TASVEG dataset combines both ecological descriptions and spatial polygon geometries. For cross-referencing purposes, we distinguish between mapping units (polygons coded by VEGCODE on the map) and vegetation communities (the ecological entities defined in the classification).
The majority of TASVEG mapping units represent distinct ecological vegetation communities—spanning coastal heathlands, wet and dry eucalypt forests, temperate rainforests, moorlands, wetlands, and alpine communities. The companion Technical Manual (Kitchener and Harris 2013) provides structured, literature-referenced ecological descriptions for each of the 159 mapping units defined in TASVEG, covering floristics, structure, environmental drivers, and disturbance regimes.
TASVEG provides several distinct resources that enter at different stages of the computational pipeline:

title: 2  Source classification: TASVEG
text:
Technical Manual (From Forest to Fjaeldmark; Kitchener and Harris (2013)): supplies the diagnostic ecological descriptions used to assess conceptual alignment (Chapter 3) and served as the primary ecological reference for all five expert interpreters during Rounds 1 and 2.
TASVEG 5.0 statewide spatial release from https://www.theLIST.tas.gov.au ©State of Tasmania (Tasmanian Vegetation Monitoring and Mapping Program 2025):

Fire attributes lookup table (.dbf): used in Chapter 4 to construct the authoritative source lookup_tbl without needing to load the full polygon geometries first.
Statewide vector spatial data (.shp and MapInfo formats): used in Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 (and in the separate output-generation scripts in Chapter 17) to compute polygon areas and generate GeoPackage and GeoTIFF outputs.
Official metadata (.pdf): documents attribute definitions, coordinate reference system (GDA94 / MGA zone 55, EPSG:28355), and release notes.

title: 2  Source classification: TASVEG
text:
2.2 Data download and attribution
TASVEG 5.0 data is supplied under the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Australia (CC BY 3.0 AU) licence.
The Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania requests attribution in the following form:

“TASVEG 5.0 from www.theLIST.tas.gov.au ©State of Tasmania”

Because the statewide shapefile archive is large and redistributed directly by theLIST Open Data, gisdata/ is excluded from Git version control. The standalone script below (scripts/TASVEG-data-download.R) checks for the local gisdata/ directory, downloads LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE.zip via wget, and extracts the shapefile and DBF lookup tables into gisdata/LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE/. Expand the code block to inspect it (not executed during book rendering):



Script to download TASVEG 5.0 data

scripts/TASVEG-data-download.R

## Download TASVEG 5.0 from www.theLIST.tas.gov.au ©State of Tasmania

## Original data description:
## > TASVEG is a comprehensive digital map of Tasmania’s vegetation, including sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island. The map depicts the extent of more than 150 vegetation communities, including coastal heathlands, eucalypt forest and alpine communities.
## > The current release version for mainland Tasmania is TASVEG 5.0 and was published in November 2025. The current release version for Macquarie Island is TASVEG 3.0 Macquarie Island and was published in November 2013.
## > Data is supplied under Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Australia (CC BY 3.0 AU) Licence http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/au/

## Recommended usage:
## R --vanilla < scripts/TASVEG-data-download.R \
##  > docs-src/reproducibility-notes/TASVEG-data-download-out.txt

## Summary of steps from data source to prepared data:
## 1. Check if data is already present
## 2. Obtaining the original data from www.theLIST.tas.gov.au
## 3. Extract target file from downloaded zip archive

## Time for action:

## 0. Setup

### Benchmarking
(start_time <- Sys.time())

### No special libraries needed

### Paths
here::i_am("scripts/TASVEG-data-download.R")
gisdata <- here::here("gisdata")
if (!dir.exists(gisdata)) {
  dir.create(gisdata)
}

# This script requires 'wget' to be installed for downloading files.
# Please install 'wget' using your package manager:
# For macOS users: brew install wget
# For Ubuntu users: sudo apt-get install wget
# For Windows users: Please refer to the wget documentation for installation instructions at:
# https://eternallybored.org/misc/wget/

## 1. Check if data is already present, and if data is complete:

completed <- FALSE

if ("LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE" %in% list.files(gisdata)) {
  cat("The folder is already present, ")
  all_files <- list.files(
    here::here(gisdata, "LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE"),
    recursive = TRUE
  )
  how_many <- length(all_files)
  cat(sprintf("there are %s files in there, ", how_many))
  if (how_many == 71) {
    cat("that sounds about right!, nothing else to do.\n")
    ## if present there is nothing to do,
    completed <- TRUE
  } else {
    if (how_many < 71) {
      cat("files missing?, will proceed to download again.\n")
      completed <- FALSE
    } else {
      cat("that's too many, please check!.\n")
      completed <- TRUE
    }
  }
}

if (!completed) {
  ## 2. Obtaining the original data from www.theLIST.tas.gov.au

  ## This is the source URL at theLIST repository
  data_url <- 'https://listdata.thelist.tas.gov.au/opendata/data/LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE.zip'

  ## Download to a tempfile
  temp_zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")

  ## very large file (1.7GB) will require sometime to download
  options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))

  ## Download with wget seems to be more stable
  download.file(
    data_url,
    destfile = temp_zip,
    mode = "wb",
    method = "wget",
    extra = c("-c")
  )

  ## 3. Extract all files from downloaded zip archive

  ## Unzip the selected file
  unzip(
    temp_zip,
    exdir = gisdata
  )
}
## Step X: Benchmarking and session info

end_time - start_time

title: 3  Assess alignment between classifications
text:
3.1 Eligibility of TASVEG mapping units
Conceptual alignment is the first principle of cross-referencing ecosystem classifications (IUCN 2025). Before estimating memberships, we must verify that units in the source classification (TASVEG 5.0) and the target classification (IUCN GET) represent comparable kinds of ecological entities (De Cáceres and Wiser 2012).
Cross-referencing elucidates relationships between units representing similar types of entities. To be eligible for cross-referencing to the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (IUCN GET; Keith et al. (2022)), source units must align with the ecosystem concept defined by the Convention on Biological Diversity (Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity 1992), following Tansley (1935):
Qualitatively different kinds of entities—such as purely abiotic land-cover masks, administrative boundaries, or coarse land-use mosaics lacking ecological specificity—should not be forced into IUCN GET functional groups. Where partial conceptual overlaps exist, units require explicit eligibility screening so that non-aligned mapping classes are flagged rather than assigned spurious memberships.
The conceptual diagram below (Figure 3.1) illustrates how diagnostic ecological descriptions from the TASVEG Technical Manual and the IUCN GET framework inform eligibility screening and fuzzy membership assignment during cross-referencing.
Most units in TASVEG 5.0 (153 of the 156 mapped statewide units, plus 3 additional codes in the Fire Attributes lookup table) represent ecological vegetation communities or recognised anthropogenic ecosystems (e.g. agricultural land, plantations, urban areas) that align well with the ecosystem concept and are therefore eligible for cross-referencing to IUCN GET Level 3 Ecosystem Functional Groups.
However, three mapping units in the broad group Other natural environments require closer scrutiny: Lichen lithosere (ORO), Sand, mud (OSM), and Water, sea (OAQ). According to the TASVEG Technical Manual (Kitchener and Harris 2013):

title: 3  Assess alignment between classifications
text:
Lichen lithosere (ORO) is important for undisturbed cryptogamic communities, such as on blockstreams, cliffs, talus and scree slopes and exposed bedrock on mountain tops and ridges.


Sand, mud (OSM) is bare of vegetation, and has been used for mapping beaches, sand dune systems, and mobile sand sheets such as those at Waterhouse in north-east Tasmania or at Sandy Cape on the west coast.


Water, sea (OAQ) has been used to designate areas of sea, artificial impoundments such as Lake Gordon, Lake Saint Clair and Lake Pedder, as well as deep water in natural lakes.


3.1.1 Eligibility decision
The units OAQ and OSM are broad, non-vegetated mapping complexes that combine multiple functionally distinct ecosystems across different IUCN GET realms and biomes—for example, OAQ merges marine waters, natural freshwater lakes, and artificial reservoirs, while OSM merges marine-terrestrial sandy beaches, intertidal mudflats, and terrestrial mobile dunes. Similarly, ORO captures exposed rock and cryptogamic lithoseres spanning disparate alpine, montane, and coastal environments that cannot be resolved into a single Ecosystem Functional Group from the TASVEG classification alone.
Without auxiliary spatial layers (such as hydrography, bathymetry, shoreline delineations, or elevation masks) to disaggregate these mapping complexes, assigning them a single statewide membership profile would introduce systematic thematic error. Consequently, OAQ, OSM, and ORO are flagged as not eligible (eligible = FALSE) in the TASVEG lookup table (Chapter 4), excluded during validation and cleaning (Chapter 6), and represented as NoData (NA) in the statewide spatial outputs (Chapter 13 and Chapter 17).

title: 4  Lookup tables for both classifications
text:
4.1 Source classification: TASVEG 5.0
Before ingesting and validating expert cross-referencing records, we construct formal lookup tables (lookup_tbl objects from the ecoSynthesis package; Ferrer-Paris, Gould, and Singh (2026)) for both the source classification (TASVEG 5.0) and the target classification (IUCN GET Level 3). These controlled vocabularies define the complete set of valid unit codes, their human-readable names, and—for the source classification—which units passed the conceptual alignment screening in Chapter 3 (eligible = TRUE vs FALSE).
For TASVEG 5.0 (Tasmanian Vegetation Monitoring and Mapping Program 2025), we build the lookup table from the official Fire Attributes .dbf table distributed with the statewide release. Using the lightweight .dbf file avoids loading the full polygon geometries during the data preparation stage.
First, we read TASVEG_5_0_Fire_Attributes_LUT.dbf with as.is = TRUE so character codes and descriptions are kept as strings rather than factors:
TASVEG_DBF <-
    read.dbf(
        here::here("..", "gisdata", "LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE", "TASVEG_5_0_Fire_Attributes_LUT.dbf"),
        as.is = TRUE
    )
From this attribute table we retain the three fields that identify each vegetation community and its higher-level TASVEG group:
Next, we select these three columns, sort them alphabetically by vegetation group and code, remove duplicate rows, and convert the result to a tibble (TASVEG_LUT):
TASVEG_LUT <-
    TASVEG_DBF |>
    select(VEG_GROUP, VEGCODE, VEGCODE_D) |>
    arrange(VEG_GROUP, VEGCODE) |>
    unique() |>
    as_tibble()
The interactive table below allows browsing and searching all 159 VEGCODE entries defined in the TASVEG 5.0 Fire Attributes table:
DT::datatable(TASVEG_LUT)
Following the conceptual alignment assessment in Chapter 3, we flag the three non-eligible mapping units (OAQ, OSM, and ORO) using the negative-matching operator %nin% from ecoSynthesis, and wrap the table into an ecoSynthesis::lookup_tbl object that stores column metadata (id, name, and eligible):
not_eligible <- c("OAQ", "OSM", "ORO")
TASVEG <- TASVEG_LUT |>

Our setup for this R session loads the DBF reader (foreign), data manipulation tools (dplyr, readr), and ecoSynthesis, and points output_dir to results/XREFs:

## 1. Check if data is already present
## 2. Obtaining the original data from www.theLIST.tas.gov.au
## 3. Extract target file from downloaded zip archive

## Time for action:

## 0. Setup

### Benchmarking
(start_time <- Sys.time())

### No special libraries needed

### Paths
here::i_am("scripts/TASVEG-data-download.R")
gisdata <- here::here("gisdata")
if (!dir.exists(gisdata)) {
  dir.create(gisdata)
}

# This script requires 'wget' to be installed for downloading files.
# Please install 'wget' using your package manager:
# For macOS users: brew install wget
# For Ubuntu users: sudo apt-get install wget
# For Windows users: Please refer to the wget documentation for installation instructions at:
# https://eternallybored.org/misc/wget/

## 1. Check if data is already present, and if data is complete:

completed <- FALSE

if ("LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE" %in% list.files(gisdata)) {
  cat("The folder is already present, ")
  all_files <- list.files(
    here::here(gisdata, "LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE"),
    recursive = TRUE
  )
  how_many <- length(all_files)
  cat(sprintf("there are %s files in there, ", how_many))
  if (how_many == 71) {
    cat("that sounds about right!, nothing else to do.\n")
    ## if present there is nothing to do,
    completed <- TRUE
  } else {
    if (how_many < 71) {
      cat("files missing?, will proceed to download again.\n")
      completed <- FALSE
    } else {

    }

}

if (!completed) {
  ## 2. Obtaining the original data from www.theLIST.tas.gov.au

  ## This is the source URL at theLIST repository
  data_url <- 'https://listdata.thelist.tas.gov.au/opendata/data/LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE.zip'

  temp_zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")

    data_url,
    destfile = temp_zip,
    mode = "wb",
    method = "wget",

4.2 Target classification: IUCN GET
The IUCN GET controlled vocabulary (Keith et al. 2022) defines all units in the upper three levels of the typology (Realms, Functional Biomes, and Ecosystem Functional Groups).

text:
5.1 Inspecting the two input layouts
The objective of this step is to ingest expert cross-referencing tables supplied in heterogeneous spreadsheet layouts and consolidate them into a single, tidy, long-format membership table suitable for validation (Chapter 6) and quantitative analysis (Chapter 8–Chapter 10).
During structured expert elicitation (Martin et al. 2012; Hemming et al. 2018), different interpreters naturally prefer different data-entry layouts — some enter candidate targets in paired columns (EFG_1, memb_1, EFG_2, memb_2, …), whereas others prefer a sparse source-by-target matrix. While both layouts are convenient for manual entry, a single long-format representation ensures interoperability across downstream validation, agreement, entropy, and synthesis functions (see Chapter 15 for a full overview of tabular formats).
We have nine CSV files in xrefdata/ covering five interpreters across two rounds of elicitation (four interpreters in Round 1 and five in Round 2). All files were prepared by MGT with a standardised 11-row metadata header (interpreter name, date, round notes) followed by a blank row and the tabular data starting on line 13, but the data tables follow two distinct shapes:

Paired-column (wide) format (seven files): each row is a VEGCODE, followed by 2 to 4 pairs of columns indicating each candidate target unit and its fuzzy membership (EFG_1, memb_1, EFG_2, memb_2, …). Below we inspect the first 15 lines of AL_V1_100626_TASVEG_5_0.csv:

title: 5  Reading input data
section: 5.2 Batch ingestion across all files and rounds
text:
5.2 Batch ingestion across all files and rounds
The loop below iterates over every CSV file in xrefdata/, reads the 11-row metadata block to extract the interpreter name (metadata[[1, 2]]) and elicitation round (metadata[11, 2]), reads the membership records starting after line 12, dispatches either pivot_wide_membership_table() (when "EFG_1" is present) or pivot_membership_matrix() (otherwise), and row-binds all files into memb_data:

memb_data <- foreach(j = dir(csv_folder), .combine = bind_rows) %do% {
    metadata <- read_csv(
        here::here(csv_folder, j),
        col_names = c("name", "value"),
        n_max = 11,
        show_col_types = FALSE
    )[, 1:2]
    data <- read_csv(here::here(csv_folder, j), skip = 12, show_col_types = FALSE)

    cat(sprintf("Read %s, interpreter %s\n%s\n", j, metadata[1, 2], metadata[11, 2]))

    if ("EFG_1" %in% colnames(data)) {
        pivot_wide_membership_table(
            xref = data,
            original_names = "VEGCODE",
            target_names = sprintf("EFG_%s", 1:4),
            membership_values = sprintf("memb_%s", 1:4),
            expert_name = metadata[[1, 2]],
            round_nr = if_else(grepl("First", metadata[11, 2]), 1, 2)
        )
    } else {
        pivot_membership_matrix(
            xref = data,
            original_names = "VEGCODE",
            target_names = colnames(data)[-1],
            expert_name = metadata[[1, 2]],
            round_nr = if_else(grepl("First", metadata[11, 2]), 1, 2)
        )
    }
}

section: 5.3 ecoSynthesis import helpers and overlap with repository functions
text:
5.3 ecoSynthesis import helpers and overlap with repository functions
The ecoSynthesis package (Ferrer-Paris, Gould, and Singh 2026) provides two dedicated helpers for importing paired-column spreadsheets:

standardise_xref_pairs() standardises non-uniform paired column names (such as GET1/GET1_p, GET2/GET2_p in raw interpreter spreadsheets) to the canonical efg_1/memb_1 convention before pivoting. Below we demonstrate this on the package’s bundled TASVEG_mini_expert_wide dataset:


standardise_xref_pairs(
    TASVEG_mini_expert_wide,
    prefix = "GET",
    suffix = "p",
    separator = "_"
) |>
    select(VEGCODE, starts_with("efg_"), starts_with("memb_")) |>
    head(4)

import_paired_membership() pivots a single paired-column data frame directly into a membership_tbl object when the exact target and membership column names are supplied. For example, on AL_V1_100626_TASVEG_5_0.csv (which contains two pairs, EFG_1–EFG_2 and memb_1–memb_2):

    here::here(csv_folder, "AL_V1_100626_TASVEG_5_0.csv"),
    skip = 12,
    show_col_types = FALSE
)

import_paired_membership(
    data = al_v1_raw,
    original_names = "VEGCODE",
    target_names = c("EFG_1", "EFG_2"),
    membership_values = c("memb_1", "memb_2"),
    interpreter = "Adelina_Latinovic"
) |>
    filter(!is.na(memb)) |>

WarningOverlap & conflict: ecoSynthesis::import_paired_membership() vs. scripts/functions.R



ecoSynthesis::import_paired_membership() overlaps directly with our repository helper pivot_wide_membership_table() in scripts/functions.R, but we intentionally retain the repository helpers (pivot_wide_membership_table() and pivot_membership_matrix()) for the batch ingestion loop above for four reasons in ecoSynthesis v0.0.0.9005:

Strict column selection: import_paired_membership() uses dplyr::all_of(c(target_names, membership_values)) and aborts if a file has fewer pairs than requested (e.g. AL_V1 has only 2 pairs rather than 4), whereas pivot_wide_membership_table() uses dplyr::any_of() and handles 2-pair and 4-pair files uniformly.
Round metadata: import_paired_membership() does not yet accept a round argument.
Output schema: import_paired_membership() always names the interpreter column "interpreter" and adds a pair index column, whereas downstream repository code uses "expert".
Matrix-format files: ecoSynthesis does not yet provide a matrix-format importer analogous to pivot_membership_matrix() for AK_V1 and AL_V2.

title: 5  Reading input data
section: 5.4 Inspecting and saving the combined table
text:
5.4 Inspecting and saving the combined table
The combined table memb_data has five columns:

VEGCODE: source unit code in TASVEG 5.0
EFG: candidate target Ecosystem Functional Group code in IUCN GET
memb: fuzzy membership value between 0 and 1
expert: interpreter name
round: elicitation round (1 = independent initial assessment; 2 = revised assessment after group discussion)

Let us inspect five random rows from memb_data:

set.seed(42)
slice_sample(memb_data, n = 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  VEGCODE EFG    memb expert            round
  <chr>   <chr> <dbl> <chr>             <dbl>
1 WDU     T3.4   0    Adelina_Latinovic     2
2 NLE     TF1.6  0.15 David_Keith           2
3 HHE     T4.5   0    Anne Kitchener        2
4 WOL     T4.4   0    Anne Kitchener        2
5 RHP     MT2.2  0    Adelina_Latinovic     2


Next, we filter out NA and zero-membership entries and count the distinct source units (VEGCODE) and distinct target units (EFG) recorded by each interpreter in each round. Notice that in Round 1, Jayne Balmer assessed a subset of 98 units and Adelina Latinovic assessed 149 (148 eligible), whereas in Round 2 all five interpreters assessed the full set of units:

memb_data |>
    filter(!is.na(memb), memb > 0) |>
    group_by(expert, round) |>
    summarise(
        `source ids` = n_distinct(VEGCODE),
        `target ids` = n_distinct(EFG),
        .groups = "drop"

title: 6  Data validation
text:
6.1 Constructing a membership_tbl object
Before calculating agreement, entropy, or spatial synthesis metrics, we must verify that every record in the consolidated membership table satisfies the structural and semantic rules of cross-referencing (IUCN 2025):
We coerce the in-memory TASVEG_xref data frame directly into an ecoSynthesis::membership_tbl object, explicitly mapping column names to the package’s semantic roles (source_id, target_id, membership, interpreter, and round). Downstream ecoSynthesis functions read these attributes automatically:
TASVEG_memb <- membership_tbl(
    TASVEG_xref,
    source_id = "VEGCODE",
    target_id = "EFG",
    membership = "memb",
    interpreter = "expert",
    round = "round"
)

title: 7  Exploration of the data
text:
7.1 Additional integrity checks
With TASVEG_clean validated against both classification lookup tables (Chapter 6), we now run a set of diagnostic checks and exploratory summaries before moving to formal agreement and entropy analyses (Chapter 8–Chapter 10). Specifically, we verify whether per-unit membership sums equal 1, check for duplicate source–target rows, examine how many candidate EFGs each TASVEG community attracts, and compare cross-referencing profiles across broad TASVEG vegetation groups.
Because check_membership() in Chapter 6 validates individual record values and IDs, we perform three group-level consistency checks across (VEGCODE, expert, round) combinations.

title: 7  Exploration of the data
8  Round one
text:
8.1 Filtering Round 1 and building a 3D membership matrix
In Round 1 of the structured expert elicitation (Martin et al. 2012; Hemming et al. 2018), four interpreters (Adelina_Latinovic, David_Keith, Jayne_Balmer, and Mark_Tozer) independently evaluated TASVEG 5.0 vegetation communities against IUCN GET Level 3 Ecosystem Functional Groups using the Technical Manual (Kitchener and Harris 2013) and IUCN cross-referencing guidelines (IUCN 2025).
Analysing Round 1 before facilitated group discussions serves two diagnostic goals:
We first filter TASVEG_clean to Round 1 and convert the long-format membership_tbl into a three-dimensional membership_matrix ([source, target, interpreter]) via ecoSynthesis::membership_matrix(). Inside this array, targets not used by an interpreter for an assessed unit are explicitly filled with 0, units an interpreter did not assess remain NA (so they are excluded from pairwise comparisons rather than treated as zeros), and any repeated (source, target, interpreter) rows (such as David_Keith on SLL, flagged in Chapter 7) are summed automatically:
TASVEG_first <- filter(TASVEG_clean, round == 1)
TASVEG_mtx_r1 <- membership_matrix(TASVEG_first)
TASVEG_mtx_r1

In Round 1, David_Keith and Mark_Tozer assessed all 153 eligible units, Adelina_Latinovic assessed 148 units, and Jayne_Balmer assessed 98 units, spanning 29 candidate EFGs in total.

title: 8  Round one
text:
8.2 Inter-interpreter agreement (calc_agreement)
For any two interpreters with membership vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) over the target EFGs for a shared source unit, ecoSynthesis::calc_agreement() computes half-\(L_1\) (Manhattan / total variation) dissimilarity:
\[D(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} |a_k - b_k|, \qquad S(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = 1 - D(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})\]
When both vectors sum to 1, \(D(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})\) equals the Bray–Curtis / Czekanowski dissimilarity (Bray and Curtis 1957) and represents the exact proportion of membership mass that would need to be reallocated to make the two profiles identical (\(S = 1\) for identical profiles; \(S = 0\) for completely disjoint target assignments).

8.2.1 Global agreement between interpreter pairs
Calling calc_agreement(TASVEG_mtx_r1) with the default by_source = FALSE returns a symmetric summary table across all interpreter pairs, reporting the number of jointly assessed units (n_units), mean and median similarity, share of virtually identical profiles (dissimilarity < 0.001), and mean dissimilarity:

8.2.2 Per-unit pairwise dissimilarity
Setting by_source = TRUE returns every unique interpreter pair per source unit (743 unit-pair comparisons in Round 1). Plotting similarity histograms faceted by interpreter pair shows how much agreement is concentrated at \(S = 1\) versus spread across partial or zero overlap:

    geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = teal_high, colour = "white") +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(interpreter_x), cols = vars(interpreter_y)) +

NoteOverlap & conflict: ecoSynthesis::calc_agreement() vs. scripts/functions.R



scripts/functions.R contains earlier prototype helpers—pairwise_dissimilarity(), summary_disagreement(), and plot_pairwise_diss()—that compute the exact same half-\(L_1\) metric \(D = \frac{1}{2}\sum_k |a_k - b_k|\) directly on a membership_tbl. Verification across all 743 Round 1 pairs and 1,530 Round 2 pairs confirms that ecoSynthesis::calc_agreement(membership_matrix(df), by_source = TRUE) produces numerically identical similarity and dissimilarity values (maximum difference \(< 10^{-9}\)).
We prefer ecoSynthesis::calc_agreement() here because it: 1. provides both global (by_source = FALSE) and per-source (by_source = TRUE) summaries in one consistent interface; 2. supports targeted subsetting via sources = and targets =; and 3. avoids a scoping bug in scripts/functions.R::plot_pairwise_diss(), which references a global variable named pd rather than its function argument x.
Note that calc_agreement()’s round argument is not yet implemented in v0.0.0.9005, so we filter TASVEG_clean to a single round before calling membership_matrix().

8.3 Target usage patterns across interpreters
Beyond pairwise scores, visualising which target EFGs each interpreter selects helps identify systematic classification preferences or isolated target choices before group discussion.
First, ecoSynthesis::membership_target_heatmap() plots how many TASVEG communities each interpreter assigned to each candidate EFG in Round 1 (empty cells indicate the interpreter never used that EFG):

    labs(title = "Round 1 Target Use")








Second, ecoSynthesis::membership_target_pair_heatmap() counts how many TASVEG communities each pair of interpreters co-assigned to the same EFG, highlighting targets with strong shared uptake versus targets invoked by only a single interpreter:

title: 8  Round one
text:
8.4 Within-interpreter uncertainty: Shannon’s entropy
While pairwise dissimilarity captures disagreement between interpreters, normalised Shannon’s entropy (Shannon 1948; Pielou 1966) captures the fuzziness or ambiguity within an interpreter’s membership vector \(\mathbf{p} = (p_1, \dots, p_N)\):
\[H_{\text{norm}}(\mathbf{p}; N) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } N \le 1 \\ -\dfrac{\sum_{k: p_k > 0} p_k \log_2(p_k)}{\log_2(N)} & \text{if } N > 1 \end{cases}\]
Depending on the normalisation denominator \(N\), ecoSynthesis computes three complementary entropy estimands:

Interpreter-normalised (\(N = S\), the number of non-zero targets selected by that interpreter): measures internal evenness—how evenly weight is split among the interpreter’s own chosen candidates.
Source-normalised (\(N = N_{\text{source}}\), total distinct candidates considered by any interpreter for that source unit): standardises interpreters evaluating the same TASVEG community against a shared candidate pool.
Set-normalised (\(N = N_{\text{set}}\), total distinct EFGs used across the whole round): standardises every profile against the full set of target groups in the dataset.


8.4.1 Worked example with calc_shannons_entropy()
Below we apply ecoSynthesis::calc_shannons_entropy() directly to Mark_Tozer’s Round 1 membership profile for FMG (Melaleuca gibbosa heathland) to illustrate how the three normalisation bases scale the same probability vector:

fmg_slice <- unclass(TASVEG_mtx_r1)["FMG", , ]
active_for_fmg <- rowSums(fmg_slice, na.rm = TRUE) > 0

p_set <- fmg_slice[, "Mark_Tozer"]
p_source <- p_set[active_for_fmg]

tibble(
    Normalisation = c(
        sprintf("Interpreter-normalised (S = %d)", sum(p_set > 0)),
        sprintf("Source-normalised (N_source = %d)", length(p_source)),
        sprintf("Set-normalised (N_set = %d)", length(p_set))
    ),
    Entropy = c(
        calc_shannons_entropy(p_source),
        calc_shannons_entropy(p_source, N = length(p_source)),
        calc_shannons_entropy(p_set, N = length(p_set))
    )
)

title: 9  Round two
text:
9.1 Filtering Round 2 and building the 3D membership matrix
Following structured group discussions of Round 1 discrepancies (Chapter 8), all interpreters revised their assignments in Round 2 (Hemming et al. 2018; IUCN 2025). Round 2 includes five interpreters (Adelina_Latinovic, Anne Kitchener, David_Keith, Jayne_Balmer, and Mark_Tozer), and every interpreter assessed the complete set of 153 eligible TASVEG 5.0 communities. Because Round 2 incorporates both shared conceptual clarification and full coverage across all five interpreters, it forms the basis for the synthesis and spatial outputs in Part III (Chapter 11–Chapter 13).
We filter TASVEG_clean to Round 2 and construct the 3D membership_matrix ([source, target, interpreter]) via ecoSynthesis::membership_matrix(). Notice that all 5 interpreters now have 153 assessed source units across 31 candidate EFGs (compared with 29 EFGs in Round 1), and Mark_Tozer’s split T4.5 entry for SWR (Chapter 7) is summed automatically inside the matrix:
TASVEG_revised <- filter(TASVEG_clean, round == 2)
TASVEG_mtx_r2 <- membership_matrix(TASVEG_revised)

9.2 Inter-interpreter agreement (calc_agreement)

9.2.1 Global agreement between interpreter pairs
Calling calc_agreement(TASVEG_mtx_r2) computes global pairwise agreement across all 10 unique interpreter pairs (mirrored symmetrically with diagonal = 1). Compared to Round 1 (Chapter 8), every pair of interpreters now compares all 153 units and achieves substantially higher mean similarity (\(\ge 0.84\) across every pair):

9.2.2 Per-unit pairwise dissimilarity
Next, calc_agreement(TASVEG_mtx_r2, by_source = TRUE) computes pairwise similarity and dissimilarity for all 1,530 unit-pair combinations (153 units × 10 interpreter pairs). The faceted histograms illustrate the strong concentration near \(S = 1\) across all ten pairs:

    group_by(VEGCODE = source) |>
    summarise(
        mean_dissimilarity = mean(dissimilarity),

        max_dissimilarity = max(dissimilarity),

        .groups = "drop"

9.3 Target usage patterns across interpreters

NotePackage caveat: hardcoded plot titles in ecoSynthesis v0.0.0.9005



Both membership_target_heatmap() (default "Round X Target Use") and membership_target_pair_heatmap() (default "Round 1 Shared Target Use") hardcode their plot titles and do not yet accept a round filter in v0.0.0.9005. Pre-filtering to round == 2 and appending + ggplot2::labs(title = ...) ensures accurate Round 2 labels without modifying package code.

title: 9  Round two
text:
9.4 Within-interpreter uncertainty: Shannon’s entropy
We next compute normalised Shannon’s entropy for Round 2 using ecoSynthesis::calc_entropy_tbl() across the entire dataset (overall), per interpreter (by_interpreter), per TASVEG community (by_source), and per target EFG (by_target).






NoteIncomplete-sum warning on HSE



Recall from Chapter 7 that Jayne_Balmer’s Round 2 profile for HSE sums to 0.90. When calc_entropy_tbl() calls calc_shannons_entropy() on that vector, ecoSynthesis emits an informative warning (sum of the probabilities is less than 1 (0.9)) and automatically re-normalises the non-zero probabilities internally (\(p_k / \sum p\)) so entropy remains strictly comparable on \([0, 1]\).

title: 10  Between rounds
text:
10.1 Comparing inter-interpreter agreement between rounds
Comparing Round 1 (Chapter 8) and Round 2 (Chapter 9) evaluates how effectively facilitated group discussion reduced inter-interpreter disagreement and reveals how interpreters adjusted their expression of fuzzy uncertainty (Martin et al. 2012; Hemming et al. 2018; IUCN 2025). Two structural differences between rounds should be kept in mind when interpreting changes:
We construct separate membership_matrix objects for Round 1 and Round 2 and compute both global (by_source = FALSE) and per-source (by_source = TRUE) agreement via ecoSynthesis::calc_agreement() (see the overlap call-out in Chapter 8 explaining why calc_agreement() is preferred over the prototype pairwise_dissimilarity() helper in scripts/functions.R):
TASVEG_first <- filter(TASVEG_clean, round == 1)
TASVEG_revised <- filter(TASVEG_clean, round == 2)

mtx1 <- membership_matrix(TASVEG_first)
mtx2 <- membership_matrix(TASVEG_revised)

ag1_global <- calc_agreement(mtx1)
ag2_global <- calc_agreement(mtx2)

ag1_unit <- calc_agreement(mtx1, by_source = TRUE)
ag2_unit <- calc_agreement(mtx2, by_source = TRUE)

title: 10  Between rounds
text:
10.1.1 Change in global agreement for returning interpreter pairs
Joining the global agreement tables across the six unique interpreter pairs present in both rounds quantifies the gain in mean similarity (delta_similarity) and share of identical unit profiles (delta_identical) following group discussion:

ag1_global |>
    filter(interpreter_x < interpreter_y) |>
    select(
        interpreter_x,
        interpreter_y,
        n_r1 = n_units,
        sim_r1 = mean_similarity,
        id_r1 = share_identical
    ) |>
    inner_join(
        ag2_global |>
            filter(interpreter_x < interpreter_y) |>
            select(
                interpreter_x,
                interpreter_y,
                n_r2 = n_units,
                sim_r2 = mean_similarity,
                id_r2 = share_identical
            ),
        by = c("interpreter_x", "interpreter_y")
    ) |>
    mutate(
        delta_similarity = round(sim_r2 - sim_r1, 3),
        delta_identical = round(id_r2 - id_r1, 3)
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(delta_similarity))

# A tibble: 6 × 10
  interpreter_x     interpreter_y  n_r1 sim_r1 id_r1  n_r2 sim_r2 id_r2
  <chr>             <chr>         <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <int>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 Adelina_Latinovic Mark_Tozer      148  0.671 0.351   153  0.859 0.405
2 Jayne_Balmer      Mark_Tozer       98  0.609 0.337   153  0.794 0.261
3 David_Keith       Mark_Tozer      153  0.680 0.261   153  0.838 0.333
4 Adelina_Latinovic David_Keith     148  0.727 0.432   153  0.842 0.444
5 David_Keith       Jayne_Balmer     98  0.697 0.429   153  0.787 0.294
6 Adelina_Latinovic Jayne_Balmer     98  0.847 0.776   153  0.853 0.484
# ℹ 2 more variables: delta_similarity <dbl>, delta_identical <dbl>


Every returning interpreter pair increased in mean similarity in Round 2 (typically by \(+0.10\) to \(+0.24\)), reflecting substantial convergence after discussing conceptual boundaries and ambiguous vegetation descriptions.


10.1.2 Unit-level shift in pairwise dissimilarity
Next, we summarise per-source disagreement for each round and join the two summaries by VEGCODE. Units falling below the 1:1 diagonal in the scatter plot experienced reduced disagreement in Round 2, while units near or above the diagonal represent persistent conceptual disagreements:

summarise_unit_disagreement <- function(ag_unit) {
    ag_unit |>
        group_by(VEGCODE = source) |>
        summarise(
            mean_dissimilarity = mean(dissimilarity),
            min_dissimilarity = min(dissimilarity),
            max_dissimilarity = max(dissimilarity),
            n_pairs = n(),
            .groups = "drop"
        )
}

dis1 <- summarise_unit_disagreement(ag1_unit)
dis2 <- summarise_unit_disagreement(ag2_unit)

dis_both <- dis1 |>
    left_join(dis2, by = "VEGCODE", suffix = c("_r1", "_r2")) |>
    mutate(
        delta_diss = mean_dissimilarity_r2 - mean_dissimilarity_r1,
        combined_rank = rank(mean_dissimilarity_r1 + mean_dissimilarity_r2)
    )

ggplot(dis_both, aes(x = mean_dissimilarity_r1, y = mean_dissimilarity_r2)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_point(
        aes(size = (n_pairs_r1 + n_pairs_r2) / 2),
        alpha = 0.7,
        colour = teal_high
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Change in per-unit mean dissimilarity between Round 1 and Round 2",
        subtitle = "Points below the dashed 1:1 line indicate improved agreement in Round 2",
        x = "Round 1 mean pairwise dissimilarity",
        y = "Round 2 mean pairwise dissimilarity",
        size = "Mean nr. of pairs"
    ) +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
    theme_wp3()








Ordering all 153 TASVEG communities by their combined dissimilarity rank and fitting LOESS smoothers for each round highlights the systematic downward shift in disagreement across almost the entire spectrum of units:

ggplot(dis_both) +
    geom_point(
        aes(x = combined_rank, y = mean_dissimilarity_r1, colour = "Round 1"),
        alpha = 0.7
    ) +
    geom_smooth(
        aes(x = combined_rank, y = mean_dissimilarity_r1, colour = "Round 1"),
        formula = y ~ x,
        method = "loess",
        span = 0.75,
        se = TRUE
    ) +
    geom_point(
        aes(x = combined_rank, y = mean_dissimilarity_r2, colour = "Round 2"),
        alpha = 0.7
    ) +
    geom_smooth(
        aes(x = combined_rank, y = mean_dissimilarity_r2, colour = "Round 2"),
        formula = y ~ x,
        method = "loess",
        span = 0.75,
        se = TRUE
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Ranked unit disagreement across elicitation rounds",
        x = "Combined dissimilarity rank (1 = lowest, 153 = highest)",
        y = "Mean pairwise dissimilarity per round"
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(
        name = "Round",
        values = c("Round 1" = "slateblue4", "Round 2" = "maroon")
    ) +
    theme_wp3()

text:
10.2 Comparing Shannon’s entropy between rounds
In addition to tracking inter-interpreter agreement, we compare normalised Shannon’s entropy across rounds directly using ecoSynthesis::calc_entropy_tbl() on the multi-round TASVEG_clean table.






NoteMulti-round grouping in ecoSynthesis::calc_entropy_tbl()

4 David_Keith           1                          0.314                   0.393
5 Jayne_Balmer          2                          0.301                   0.350
6 Anne Kitchener        2                          0.154                   0.205
7 Adelina_Latinovic     2                          0.146                   0.194
8 Adelina_Latinovic     1                          0.0912                  0.128
9 Jayne_Balmer          1                          0                       0    
# ℹ abbreviated names: ¹​mean_by_interpreter_entropy_source_normalised,
#   ²​mean_by_interpreter_entropy_interpreter_normalised
# ℹ 1 more variable: mean_by_interpreter_entropy_set_normalised <dbl>


Plotting interpreter-level mean source-normalised entropy across rounds shows an instructive pattern: while inter-interpreter disagreement dropped sharply in Round 2, within-interpreter entropy increased for Jayne_Balmer (who moved from exclusively 100% single-EFG assignments in Round 1 to fuzzy multi-EFG profiles in Round 2) and Adelina_Latinovic, whereas Mark_Tozer’s entropy decreased slightly as assignments sharpened:

ggplot(
    ent_by_interp,
    aes(
        x = expert,
        y = mean_by_interpreter_entropy_source_normalised,
        fill = factor(round)
    )
) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65) +
    scale_fill_manual(
        name = "Round",
        values = c("1" = "slateblue4", "2" = "maroon")
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Mean source-normalised Shannon's entropy by interpreter and round",
        x = "Interpreter",
        y = "Mean source-normalised entropy"
    ) +
    theme_wp3() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))








Next, we reshape unit-level source-normalised entropy (overall = "by_source") wide by round to compare how individual TASVEG units shifted in within-interpreter fuzziness between rounds:

ent_by_source <- calc_entropy_tbl(TASVEG_clean, overall = "by_source")

ent_wide <- ent_by_source |>
    select(VEGCODE, round, entropy = mean_by_source_entropy_source_normalised) |>
    pivot_wider(
        names_from = round,
        values_from = entropy,
        names_prefix = "entropy_r"
    )

ggplot(ent_wide, aes(x = entropy_r1, y = entropy_r2)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, colour = "#355C7D") +
    labs(
        title = "Change in per-unit source-normalised entropy between rounds",
        x = "Round 1 mean source-normalised entropy",
        y = "Round 2 mean source-normalised entropy"
    ) +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
    theme_wp3()

title: 10  Between rounds
section: 10.3 Disagreement vs. fuzziness: decomposing Round 2 uncertainty
text:
10.3 Disagreement vs. fuzziness: decomposing Round 2 uncertainty
Combining Round 2 mean pairwise dissimilarity (inter-interpreter disagreement) with Round 2 mean source-normalised entropy (within-interpreter fuzziness) separates three distinct ecological regimes across the 153 TASVEG communities:

Bottom-left (low dissimilarity, low entropy): crisp, high-consensus 1:1 mappings to a single IUCN GET EFG.
Top-left (low dissimilarity, high entropy): consensual fuzziness — interpreters agree with one another that the TASVEG community is inherently transitional or composite across multiple EFGs.
Right (high dissimilarity): contested units where interpreters still hold diverging conceptual assignments after Round 2 discussions.


uncertainty_r2 <- dis2 |>
    left_join(
        ent_by_source |>
            filter(round == 2) |>
            select(
                VEGCODE,
                mean_entropy = mean_by_source_entropy_source_normalised
            ),
        by = "VEGCODE"
    )

ggplot(uncertainty_r2, aes(x = mean_dissimilarity, y = mean_entropy)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.75, colour = "#84659A", size = 2.5) +
    geom_text(
        data = filter(
            uncertainty_r2,
            mean_dissimilarity > 0.35 | mean_entropy > 0.75
        ),
        aes(label = VEGCODE),
        nudge_y = 0.03,
        size = 3,
        check_overlap = TRUE
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Round 2: Disagreement vs. within-interpreter entropy",
        subtitle = "Crisp consensus (bottom-left), consensual fuzziness (top-left), and contested units (right)",
        x = "Round 2 mean pairwise dissimilarity",
        y = "Round 2 mean source-normalised entropy"
    ) +
    theme_wp3()












Hemming, Victoria, Mark A. Burgman, Anca M. Hanea, Marissa F. McBride, and Bonnie C. Wintle. 2018. “A Practical Guide to Structured Expert Elicitation Using the IDEA Protocol.” Methods in Ecology and Evolution 9 (1): 169–80. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12857.


IUCN. 2025. Standards, Methods and Guidelines for Cross-Referencing Ecosystem Classifications and Maps to the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (version Version 1.0). Edited by D. A. Keith, A. Dayaram, A. Driver, J. R. Ferrer-Paris, R. Francis, S. Hay, N. J. Murray, et al. Gland, Switzerland: IUCN. https://doi.org/10.2305/CPPC6126.


Martin, Tara G., Mark A. Burgman, Fiona Fidler, Petra M. Kuhnert, Samantha Low-Choy, Marissa McBride, and Kerrie Mengersen. 2012. “Eliciting Expert Knowledge in Conservation Science.” Conservation Biology 26 (1): 29–38. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2011.01806.x.

title: 11  Synthesis overview
text:
11.1 Four synthesis table variants
The objective of the synthesis stage (Step 5 of Figure 1.1; IUCN (2025)) is to consolidate validated membership assessments from multiple interpreters into structured summary tables ready for area accounting (Chapter 12) and spatial mapping (Chapter 13 and Chapter 17).
Using the cleaned membership table (TASVEG_clean) as our authoritative input, several explicit design decisions govern how information is aggregated:
Combining the interpreter and candidate-retention choices yields four distinct summary structures explored below:

title: 11  Synthesis overview
text:
Strategy
Interpreters
Aggregation metric
Candidates kept
Ranking rule
Weighting rule




1. Full Round 2 records
All (separate)
None
All non-zero candidates
None (flags best)
Individual membership (memb)


2. Aggregated, all candidates
Aggregated
prop_memb
All non-zero candidates
None (flags best)
prop_memb


3. Best candidate per interpreter
All (separate)
None

Highest memb
None (“winner takes all”)


4. Best candidate from summary
Aggregated
prop_memb
Single best per VEGCODE
Highest prop_memb
None (“winner takes all”)





Our setup for this R session loads ecoSynthesis, dplyr, sf, units, and ggplot2, and reads the validated membership table from results/XREFs/memb-tables.rda:

library(sf)
library(ecoSynthesis)
library(dplyr)
library(units)
library(ggplot2)
here::i_am("synthesis/index.qmd")
output_dir <- here::here("../results/XREFs")
load(here::here(output_dir, "memb-tables.rda"))


11.1.1 1. Keep all individual Round 2 records
The first option preserves every validated positive record from Round 2 without aggregating across interpreters. Within each (VEGCODE, expert) pair, we compute the interpreter’s total assigned membership (total_memb), flag their highest-scoring candidate (best), and set unit-level support counters (supporting = 1, total_interp = 1) for schema consistency with aggregated tables:

TASVEG_revised <- TASVEG_clean |>
    filter(round == 2) |>
    group_by(VEGCODE, expert) |>
    mutate(
        total_memb = sum(memb),
        best = memb == max(memb),
        supporting = 1,
        total_interp = 1
    ) |>
    ungroup()

Inspecting AAP (Alkaline pans) shows all individual Round 2 assignments across the five interpreters:

TASVEG_revised |>
    filter(VEGCODE == "AAP")

# A tibble: 7 × 9
  VEGCODE EFG    memb expert      round total_memb best  supporting total_interp
  <chr>   <chr> <dbl> <chr>       <dbl>      <dbl> <lgl>      <dbl>        <dbl>
1 AAP     TF1.7   1   Anne Kitch…     2          1 TRUE           1            1
2 AAP     TF1.7   1   Adelina_La…     2          1 TRUE           1            1
3 AAP     TF1.7   0.8 David_Keith     2          1 TRUE           1            1
4 AAP     F2.8    0.2 David_Keith     2          1 FALSE          1            1
5 AAP     TF1.7   1   Jayne_Balm…     2          1 TRUE           1            1
6 AAP     TF1.7   0.9 Mark_Tozer      2          1 TRUE           1            1
7 AAP     TF1.6   0.1 Mark_Tozer      2          1 FALSE          1            1




11.1.2 2. Aggregate across interpreters, keeping all candidates
When a single multi-interpreter consensus profile is needed while still preserving fuzzy secondary relationships (for example, to generate the per-EFG membership rasters in Output 2; Chapter 17), we call ecoSynthesis::summarise_membership() with keep_all = TRUE and which_round = 2, then add a best flag identifying each community’s top-ranked EFG:

TASVEG_summary <-
    TASVEG_clean |>
    summarise_membership(keep_all = TRUE, which_round = 2) |>
    mutate(
        best = prop_memb == max(prop_memb),
        .by = VEGCODE
    )

Round nr. 2 selected.








NoteecoSynthesis::summarise_membership() default argument note



In ecoSynthesis v0.0.0.9005, the function signature defaults to keep_all = TRUE, whereas its documentation text describes keep_all = FALSE as the default. Passing keep_all = TRUE or keep_all = FALSE explicitly avoids ambiguity.


For AAP, aggregation reduces the individual records to three candidate EFGs, with TF1.7 receiving prop_memb = 0.94 from all five interpreters (supporting = 5) and two minor candidates receiving small weights:

TASVEG_summary |>
    filter(VEGCODE == "AAP")

── <membership_summary> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


ℹ source_id column: `VEGCODE`


ℹ target_id column: `EFG`


✔ `summarise_membership(data = TASVEG_clean, keep_all = TRUE, which_round = 2)`


# A tibble: 3 × 8
  VEGCODE EFG   round prop_memb total_memb supporting total_interp best 
  <chr>   <chr> <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>      <int>        <int> <lgl>
1 AAP     TF1.7     2      0.94          5          5            5 TRUE 
2 AAP     F2.8      2      0.04          5          1            5 FALSE
3 AAP     TF1.6     2      0.02          5          1            5 FALSE


Notice that prop_memb differs from the simple mean of non-zero records in the long-format table, because the long table omits implicit zero memberships from interpreters who did not select a minor candidate:

TASVEG_revised |>
    filter(VEGCODE == "AAP") |>
    summarise(
        mean_nonzero_memb = mean(memb),
        nr_interpreters = n_distinct(expert),
        .by = all_of("EFG")
    )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  EFG   mean_nonzero_memb nr_interpreters
  <chr>             <dbl>           <int>
1 TF1.7              0.94               5
2 F2.8               0.2                1
3 TF1.6              0.1                1


Instead, computing row means across interpreters from the 3D ecoSynthesis::membership_matrix()—where unused targets for assessed units are explicitly filled with 0—matches prop_memb whenever every interpreter’s profile sums to 1.0:

aap_mat <- unclass(membership_matrix(filter(TASVEG_clean, round == 2)))["AAP", , ]
rowMeans(aap_mat, na.rm = TRUE) |>
    (\(x) x[x > 0])()

 F2.8 TF1.6 TF1.7 
 0.04  0.02  0.94 




11.1.3 3. Keep the best candidate per interpreter
A third option retains one categorical “best” EFG per (VEGCODE, expert) combination via slice_max(..., with_ties = FALSE, n = 1), preserving inter-interpreter variation in categorical assignments while discarding minority fuzzy weights:

TASVEG_best_revised <-
    TASVEG_revised |>
    slice_max(memb, by = c(VEGCODE, expert), with_ties = FALSE, n = 1) |>
    mutate(keep = "best")

For AAP, all five interpreters agree on TF1.7 as their top candidate, though their individual membership strengths range between 0.8 and 1.0:

TASVEG_best_revised |>
    filter(VEGCODE == "AAP")

# A tibble: 5 × 10
  VEGCODE EFG    memb expert      round total_memb best  supporting total_interp
  <chr>   <chr> <dbl> <chr>       <dbl>      <dbl> <lgl>      <dbl>        <dbl>
1 AAP     TF1.7   1   Anne Kitch…     2          1 TRUE           1            1
2 AAP     TF1.7   1   Adelina_La…     2          1 TRUE           1            1
3 AAP     TF1.7   0.8 David_Keith     2          1 TRUE           1            1
4 AAP     TF1.7   1   Jayne_Balm…     2          1 TRUE           1            1
5 AAP     TF1.7   0.9 Mark_Tozer      2          1 TRUE           1            1
# ℹ 1 more variable: keep <chr>




11.1.4 4. Keep the single best candidate from the aggregated summary
Finally, for single-layer categorical maps (such as the 90 m Best-Candidate Spatial Synthesis in Output 3; Chapter 17), calling summarise_membership(TASVEG_clean, keep_all = FALSE, which_round = 2) selects the single EFG with the highest prop_memb for each of the 153 eligible TASVEG units:

TASVEG_best_summary <-
    summarise_membership(TASVEG_clean, keep_all = FALSE, which_round = 2)

Round nr. 2 selected.


Inspecting AAP returns a single row (TF1.7, prop_memb = 0.94, supporting = 5 of 5):

TASVEG_best_summary |>
    filter(VEGCODE == "AAP")

── <membership_summary> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


ℹ source_id column: `VEGCODE`


ℹ target_id column: `EFG`


✔ `summarise_membership(data = TASVEG_clean, keep_all = FALSE, which_round = 2)`


# A tibble: 1 × 7
  VEGCODE EFG   round prop_memb total_memb supporting total_interp
  <chr>   <chr> <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>      <int>        <int>
1 AAP     TF1.7     2      0.94          5          5            5


Rounding prop_memb to one decimal place and tallying distinct VEGCODE counts per EFG summarises how strongly supported the best-candidate assignments are across all 21 winning IUCN GET functional groups:

TASVEG_best_summary |>
    mutate(memb = round(prop_memb, 1)) |>
    group_by(EFG, memb) |>
    summarise(n = n_distinct(VEGCODE), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 59 × 3
   EFG     memb     n

We save all four synthesis tables (TASVEG_revised, TASVEG_summary, TASVEG_best_revised, and TASVEG_best_summary) to results/XREFs/memb-summaries.rda for downstream area calculations (Chapter 12) and standalone output scripts (Chapter 17):

save(
    TASVEG_revised,
    TASVEG_summary,
    TASVEG_best_revised,
    TASVEG_best_summary,
    file = here::here(output_dir, "memb-summaries.rda")
)

title: 11  Synthesis overview
section: 11.2 Connecting tabular synthesis to spatial outputs
text:
11.2 Connecting tabular synthesis to spatial outputs
The tabular summaries above serve as intermediate inputs for spatial operations: joining them back to the attribute table of the TASVEG 5.0 polygons (TASVEG_5_0.shp) enables both non-spatial area accounting (Chapter 12) and spatial raster/vector products (Chapter 13). Depending on the output format—a single categorical GeoTIFF, a multi-layer stack of per-EFG membership rasters, or a vector GeoPackage bundle—different amounts of fuzzy and per-interpreter information can be preserved (see Chapter 17).




IUCN. 2025. Standards, Methods and Guidelines for Cross-Referencing Ecosystem Classifications and Maps to the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (version Version 1.0). Edited by D. A. Keith, A. Dayaram, A. Driver, J. R. Ferrer-Paris, R. Francis, S. Hay, N. J. Murray, et al. Gland, Switzerland: IUCN. https://doi.org/10.2305/CPPC6126.

title: 12  Area summaries
12  Area summaries
text:
12.2 Individual-interpreter weighted area estimates
In cross-referencing area calculations, each TASVEG VEGCODE occurs across many map polygons, and each VEGCODE may carry fuzzy membership to multiple target EFGs. This workflow assumes that the source-to-target membership vector applies uniformly across all polygons belonging to the same VEGCODE.
First, we perform a many-to-many left join between TASVEG_areas and the individual Round 2 assessments (TASVEG_revised), coding non-eligible polygons (OAQ, OSM, ORO) explicitly as "!XREF":

EFG_memb_exp_areas <- TASVEG_areas |> # nolint: object_name_linter.
    left_join(TASVEG_revised, by = "VEGCODE", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    mutate(EFG = coalesce(EFG, "!XREF"))

To incorporate cross-referencing uncertainty into extent estimates, we compare:

Unweighted total area (\(\sum \text{area}\)): full extent of every polygon with positive membership to the target EFG.
Membership-weighted area (\(\sum \text{area} \times \text{memb}\)): scales each polygon’s contribution by its fuzzy membership proportion.

Using T2.5 (Temperate pyric humid forests) as a concrete example, we summarise unweighted and weighted areas (in \(\text{km}^2\)) by interpreter and whether T2.5 is the best candidate (best = TRUE) or a secondary candidate (best = FALSE):

EFG_memb_exp_areas |>
    filter(EFG == "T2.5") |>
    summarise(
        nr_VEGCODE = n_distinct(VEGCODE),
        mean_memb = mean(memb),
        area_total = set_units(sum(area), "km2"),
        area_weighted = set_units(sum(area * memb), "km2"),
        .by = c(expert, EFG, best)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(area_total))

# A tibble: 10 × 7
   expert            EFG   best  nr_VEGCODE mean_memb area_total area_weighted
   <chr>             <chr> <lgl>      <int>     <dbl>     [km^2]        [km^2]
 1 Anne Kitchener    T2.5  TRUE          24     0.969     12730.        12381.
 2 Adelina_Latinovic T2.5  TRUE          24     0.972     12730.        12411.
 3 David_Keith       T2.5  TRUE          26     0.783     13066.        10660.
 4 Jayne_Balmer      T2.5  TRUE          22     0.975     12400.        12149.
 5 Mark_Tozer        T2.5  TRUE          24     0.851     12809.        11287.
 6 Anne Kitchener    T2.5  FALSE          6     0.327      2465.          825.
 7 Adelina_Latinovic T2.5  FALSE          7     0.325      2491.          827.
 8 David_Keith       T2.5  FALSE          5     0.104      3729.          397.
 9 Mark_Tozer        T2.5  FALSE          7     0.131      5812.          681.
10 Jayne_Balmer      T2.5  FALSE         11     0.147      6077.          789.


Because interpreters assign slightly different sets of secondary communities and fuzzy weights to T2.5, both the unweighted and weighted area estimates vary across interpreters.
To inspect which individual TASVEG units drive that difference, we aggregate polygon areas to km² per (expert, VEGCODE), split each unit’s total area into assigned_area (\(\text{area} \times \text{memb}\)) and remaining_area (\(\text{area} \times (1 - \text{memb})\)), and reshape long for stacked bar plotting:

plot_data <- EFG_memb_exp_areas |>
    filter(EFG == "T2.5") |>
    summarise(
        total_area = sum(drop_units(set_units(area, "km2"))),
        .by = all_of(c("expert", "VEGCODE", "memb", "best"))
    ) |>
    mutate(
        sid = reorder(VEGCODE, total_area),
        assigned_area = total_area * memb,
        remaining_area = total_area - assigned_area
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = c(assigned_area, remaining_area),
        names_to = "segment",
        values_to = "height"
    ) |>
    mutate(segment = factor(segment, levels = c("remaining_area", "assigned_area"))) |>
    arrange(sid)

Plotting all units assigned positive membership to T2.5 faceted by interpreter reveals that several spatially extensive TASVEG communities carry only low secondary membership weights—contributing substantially to unweighted area totals while adding only modestly to weighted area estimates:

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = sid, y = height, fill = segment)) +
    geom_col(position = "stack") +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("assigned_area" = "#db349e", "remaining_area" = "#e1a6cb"),
        labels = c("assigned_area" = "Assigned (area * memb)", "remaining_area" = "Remaining area")
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "TASVEG units assigned to T2.5 by interpreter (all candidates)",
        x = "Source units ordered by total area",
        y = "Area (km²)",
        fill = "Component"
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~expert) +
    theme_wp3() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = 6))








Restricting the same chart to units where T2.5 is the best candidate (best == TRUE) removes those low-weight secondary communities and highlights the high-consensus core communities of T2.5:

ggplot(filter(plot_data, best), aes(x = sid, y = height, fill = segment)) +
    geom_col(position = "stack") +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("assigned_area" = "#db349e", "remaining_area" = "#e1a6cb"),
        labels = c("assigned_area" = "Assigned (area * memb)", "remaining_area" = "Remaining area")
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "TASVEG units assigned to T2.5 by interpreter (best candidate only)",
        x = "Source units ordered by total area",
        y = "Area (km²)",
        fill = "Component"
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~expert) +
    theme_wp3() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1, size = 7))

title: 12  Area summaries
12  Area summaries
section: 12.4 Statewide comparison across all IUCN GET functional groups
text:
12.4 Statewide comparison across all IUCN GET functional groups
Finally, we compute weighted area estimates across all candidate EFGs for both individual interpreters (d1, hollow circles) and the aggregated consensus (d2, filled circles), keeping primary (best == TRUE) and secondary (best == FALSE) contributions distinct:

d1 <- EFG_memb_exp_areas |>
    summarise(
        nr_VEGCODE = n_distinct(VEGCODE),
        mean_memb = mean(memb),
        area_total = set_units(sum(area), "km2"),
        area_weighted = set_units(sum(area * memb), "km2"),
        .by = c(expert, EFG, best)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(area_total))

d2 <- EFG_memb_agg_areas |>
    summarise(
        nr_VEGCODE = n_distinct(VEGCODE),
        mean_memb = mean(prop_memb),
        area_total = set_units(sum(area), "km2"),
        area_weighted = set_units(sum(area * prop_memb), "km2"),
        .by = c(EFG, best)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(area_total))

plot_data_all <- bind_rows(d1, d2)

Plotting membership-weighted area on a \(\log_{10}\) scale across all EFGs shows (1) how tightly individual interpreter extent estimates cluster around the aggregated consensus for dominant terrestrial EFGs, and (2) which EFGs exist purely as secondary components (best = FALSE, e.g. minor wetland or freshwater functional groups) versus dominant mapped ecosystems (best = TRUE):

ggplot(plot_data_all) +
    geom_point(
        aes(
            y = EFG,
            x = drop_units(area_weighted),
            shape = is.na(expert),
            colour = best
        ),
        size = 3.5,
        alpha = 0.85
    ) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_colour_manual(
        values = c("FALSE" = "peru", "TRUE" = "orchid4"),
        na.value = "grey50",
        name = "Is best candidate?"
    ) +
    scale_shape_manual(
        values = c("TRUE" = 19, "FALSE" = 21),
        labels = c("TRUE" = "Aggregated consensus", "FALSE" = "Individual interpreter"),
        name = "Estimate type"
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Statewide membership-weighted area across all candidate EFGs",
        x = "Membership-weighted area (km², log10 scale)",
        y = "IUCN GET Ecosystem Functional Group (EFG)"
    ) +
    theme_wp3()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).













Pebesma, Edzer. 2018. “Simple Features for R: Standardized Support for Spatial Vector Data.” The R Journal 10 (1): 439–46. https://doi.org/10.32614/RJ-2018-009.

title: 13  Spatial outputs
13  Spatial outputs
text:
Best-candidate (“winner-takes-all”) synthesis (keep_all = FALSE) creates a strict many-to-one join to polygons, allowing the entire state to be represented by three compact 90 m raster layers (best-candidate EFG pixel code, prop_memb, and supporting interpreter count; Output 3 in Chapter 17).
All-candidates synthesis (keep_all = TRUE) creates a many-to-many relationship, requiring either one raster layer per candidate EFG (31 GeoTIFFs; Output 2) or a polygon vector GeoPackage for a selected EFG or bundled interpreter matrices (Output 1 and Derived Outputs in Chapter 17).

title: 13  Spatial outputs
text:
13.2 Best-candidate synthesis join
Here we aggregate Round 2 assessments to a single best-candidate EFG per VEGCODE via ecoSynthesis::summarise_membership(keep_all = FALSE, which_round = 2):

TASVEG_best_summary <-
    summarise_membership(TASVEG_clean, keep_all = FALSE, which_round = 2)

Round nr. 2 selected.


Next, we join TASVEG_best_summary onto TASVEG_xy (many-to-one on VEGCODE) and attach the standard Global Ecosystems Atlas integer pixel codes (efg_pixel_value) from geco::geco_efg_data():

    left_join(TASVEG_best_summary, by = "VEGCODE", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
    left_join(efg_pixel_values, by = "EFG")

title: 13  Spatial outputs
text:
13.3 Rasterisation workflow (illustrative; executed separately)
The code block below illustrates how the standalone script scripts/TASVEG-xref-IUCNGET-output-best-90m.R rasterises TASVEG_xy_best onto a 90 m × 90 m grid (EPSG:28355) using fasterize::fasterize()—chosen over terra::rasterize() based on the speed benchmarks in Chapter 16—attaches the official Global Ecosystems Atlas colour table (coltab()) and GDAL metadata tags (metags()), and writes the GeoTIFFs. It is marked eval: false so it is not re-executed during book rendering:

rez <- 90
TASVEG_raster <- raster::raster(TASVEG_xy, res = rez)

# Rasterise best-candidate membership proportion, EFG pixel code, and support count
memb_raster <- fasterize(
    TASVEG_xy_best,
    TASVEG_raster,
    field = "prop_memb",
    fun = "max"
) |> rast()

target_raster <- fasterize(
    TASVEG_xy_best,
    TASVEG_raster,
    field = "efg_pixel_value",
    fun = "first"
) |> rast()

supp_raster <- fasterize(
    TASVEG_xy_best,
    TASVEG_raster,
    field = "supporting",
    fun = "max"
) |> rast()

# Embed Global Ecosystems Atlas colour table and GDAL metadata tags
ctab <- geco_efg_data() |> transmute(value = efg_pixel_value, color = efg_hex_code)
coltab(target_raster) <- ctab

rast_metadata <- c(
    PROJECT = "Ecosystem Indicators Workflows",
    TITLE = "Best candidate ecosystem functional group",
    DESCRIPTION = "Synthesis of crossreference from TASVEG 5.0 to IUCN GET"
)
metags(target_raster) <- rast_metadata

writeRaster(
    target_raster,
    here::here(best_dir, "TASVEG-xref-target.tiff"),
    overwrite = TRUE
)

title: 13  Spatial outputs
text:
13.5 Multi-layer EFG membership raster stacks (illustrative)
When all 31 candidate EFGs are rasterised separately into individual 90 m membership layers (scripts/EFG-membership-raster.R → results/efg-membership-rasters/; Output 2 in Chapter 17), the full stack can be read into terra to cross-check the dominant layer index (which.max) and maximum membership (max) per pixel across all layers. Because pixel-wise terra::app() over 31 statewide 90 m rasters is computationally slow, these diagnostic commands are shown with eval: false:

efg_rast_dir <- here::here("../results/efg-membership-rasters")
tas_all <- rast(dir(efg_rast_dir, pattern = "-memb-90m\\.tiff$", full.names = TRUE))

# Identify which EFG layer achieves the highest prop_memb at each 90 m pixel
tas_which <- app(tas_all, fun = "which.max", na.rm = TRUE)
plot(tas_which, main = "Layer index of maximum EFG membership")

# Compute the maximum prop_memb value across all 31 candidate EFG layers
tas_max <- app(tas_all, fun = "max", na.rm = TRUE)
plot(tas_max, main = "Maximum EFG membership across all 31 layers")
